## From EVs to Robots: China’s Edge in Physical AI


November 23, 2026


Our Chief China Equity Strategist Laura Wang is joined by Tim Hsiao, Head of Greater China Auto and Mobility Research, and Sheng Zhong, Head of China Industrial Research, to discuss how the country’s supply chain, manufacturing scale and real-world data could accelerate AI adoption in cars and robots.


*This report references export controls and/or entities that may be subject to export control restrictions. Readers are solely responsible for ensuring that their investment or trade activities are carried out in compliance with applicable laws.*


## Transcript


**Laura Wang:** Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Laura Wang, Chief China Equity Strategist at Morgan Stanley Research. And on this very special episode of the podcast, we're coming to you directly from Morgan Stanley's Asia Pacific Summit in Singapore to discuss the physical AI revolution: how China is bringing AI to the real world.


I'm joined by Tim Hsiao, Head of Greater China Auto and Mobility Research, and Sheng Zhong, Head of China Industrial Research. And with that, let's get started.


So, I want to start with Sheng Zhong. So, you covered the robots, the humanoids, all the exciting things, right? I want to understand – because for those things to work, we do not only need the brain. We actually need the components, the parts, the batteries, the motors, the actuators, all to work together.


Do you think that's where China is really differentiated versus the rest of the competitors? And where do you see the biggest gaps that still needs to be closed?


**Sheng Zhong:** We do think China ha\[s\] a unique advantage in the physical AI and also robotics.


It's not only about the frontier AI model, it's more about the manufacturing. It's more about the supply chain.


So, we think China's uniqueness and advantage lies in its vast supply chain and also the application scenarios. So, the supply chain built in the past decades from the smartphone, from the EVs, renewable energy, they can be used in the robotics. And then the robotics, they need \[to\] collect the physical data from their application to the real work scenario.


So, China, I think, ha\[s\] vast working scenarios that can collect the data and then flywheel to the robot development. So, I think that is \[a\] very unique advantage.


We still think the foundation model of embodied AI is also a very important part. And, on this perspective, we think China still ha\[s\] the constraint from the advanced chips and more advanced frontier models.


That is the gap. I think China need\[s\] to catch up and need\[s\] to close more and combine it with the hardware side.


**Laura Wang:** Thanks very much, Sheng. And the next question would be for Tim. Tim, you've covered auto industry for many years, and we understand that in the past, cars are more competing in terms of designs, the driving experience, and the energy efficiency particularly. But now as we enter the physical AI world, what do you think is shifting by introducing this physical AI into the car industry?


**Tim Hsiao:** So, we do think the whole dynamics has been changing because the physical AI, will change the competitive landscape over the next three years. So, I think in China Auto, China EV, bring in physical AI on the road at scale.


So, it combine\[s\] the real-world data you can collect every day. It combine\[s\] the advanced manufacturing. It combine\[s\] the paying customers. So, all this together, basically, can be used or put on the millions of the connected machines that can learn, can sense, can act every day.


In the meantime, I think physical AI also bring in the China EV scaled into a bigger commercial opportunity. Because nowadays, with the AI, I think the car can earn more and the factory can cost less. So, on the road, for example, you look at the smart EVs, the launch over the past few years, they basically combine the sensor computing and also the motion control software. And it's for daily use.


I think a couple years ago, it's basically it's hard to imagine it would happen, but nowadays, you can easily buy older cars in China. So I think, competition-wise, it's no longer about design. I think design is still very important. But beyond that, I think the functionality, technology features and the data, the autonomous driving and the human-machine interface will be getting more importance.


And on the other side, would be the manufacturing. I think the physical AI will basically, help China to make their manufacturing expertise more transferable. Because one of the major reasons is that if you think about what happened to the China auto industry this year, we are looking for the export. The vehicle export to reach nine to 10 million.


So that implies about 50 to 60 percent year-over-year volume increase. But of course, to sustain this kind of growth over time, you can't just simply rely on export. You need to localize the production. So, we do believe that the physical AIs or AI-guided manufacturing could help to – to handle this kind of diverse workforce scale and to minimize the cultural shock. And to improve the efficiency, to improve the quality, and reduce the cost.


So, we do believe that in the future, for the globalization, I think AI will also play a very important role to facilitate, the auto industry's global extension.


**Laura Wang:** So as we walk through 2026, investors actually have all experienced a quick transition or shift of trades from the AI infrastructure to the adoption layer and to the different channels for AI diffusion.


So I think the entire market is looking for where the physical AI or the next AI diffusion channel that can really scale. Do you think intelligent vehicles would be the next largest thing that could happen to AI diffusion? And what would make it work, particularly commercially?


**Tim Hsiao:** I do believe that the auto, especially smart EV, would be one of the key platforms for this kind of physical AI adoptions. One of the major reason is that, each year I think we have around 20 millions the cars sold in China. Probably three years ago, I would say probably just 10 - 15 percent of these were smart EV. But nowadays I would say more than 90 percent of these have the smart features.


So, the majority of the cars, they combine the sensors, combine the computing units, they combine the software, they combine the motion controls; all these kind of smart features, into the car.


More importantly, the thing about the whole usage scenario is not only for the passenger vehicles. But it also empower\[s\] the commercial vehicles for logistic, for the truck, for, for vans.


So, there are actually a lot of opportunity because one of the key debate is that we have the software, we have the technology, but we don't have use case. But in China, we are using that every day.


And we'd expect the penetration to reach 50 percent by 2030.


As we think about one of the hottest topic\[s\] these days – robotaxi. We are looking for 46,000 of robotaxi in China by 2028. And it could achieve; easily achieve one million by 2035.


So, all this together make us believe that we are no longer talking about the transportation. It's become the tech devices and that's one of the major reason\[s\] I'm very confident.


It’s definitely a strong candidate for the physical AI deployment in the upcoming years.


**Laura Wang:** Sheng, I want to bring the discussion back to you. when we think about humanoids, that's very different from cars. \[Be\]cause cars, at the end of the day, still bring people from one point to another point, right? There is a very specific purpose of using cars. But what about humanoids, particularly those are the human-shaped robots.


Robots itself is not a new concept.


But why do we have to be so stuck with this human-shaped robot idea? What better economics can humanoids bring to the table?


**Sheng Zhong:** Yeah. So, basically you see a lot of industrial robot and some moving robot everywhere in the warehouse, in the factories. I think that is increased the productivity greatly already. And this is what people \[are\] always asking. Why \[do\] we still need humanoids? So, if you look at the industrial robot and other robot. They are more worked in the structured environment: in factory, in warehouse, in the ports. But our world is non-structured in most of cases. At your home, at service areas… Then a humanoid that can be a better format in these scenarios, in my view.


So that is why we need humanoid that \[does\] not only assist people/human. But that can do a lot of work instead of human.


**Laura Wang:** So now I want to actually try to bring the robot discussion and the auto discussion together. So, talking about scalability, and if we think about how China has the largest EV fleet in the world.


So how can we think about how the EV industry or the training, the driving, and all the data that's happening on a daily basis can actually help the robot industry? Tim to you.


**Tim Hsiao:** Yeah. Probably I just a kickstart; for scale matters because data matters. So, if you think about the smart EV fleet in China because it's such a huge size of fleet. They will encounter diverse weathers, the driving conditions, the traffic, and driving behaviors.


And that they can help then to collect a lot of different data and quality data that can further help training, inferencing, and validation. For example, one vehicle probably can collect 10 hours useful data.


If you think about the one million cars, we can get probably 36.5 billion useful hours data. And today, I think \[in\] China, there are probably 45 to 50 million NEVs fleet.


And going forward, for now, the majority of the cars are still running on China or in the major cities. But, with the overseas or global expansion, we do believe that a more EV startup or a car maker can bring the smart EV to the overseas market, to collect even more diverse data, which can further enhance the smart mobility.


**Laura Wang:** So, within the auto industry, and when we talk about physical AI, we have privately owned cars, we have commercial fleet, and we have robotaxis.


So, if we think about these three different, sort of, you know, opportunity sets, where do you think the commerciality could first materialize? And why is that?


**Tim Hsiao:** So, in our view, I think hardware component suppliers would be the early beneficiary. Because one of the major reasons, as I just mentioned, to achieve the certain, like a level two, level three, or even like a level four functionality. You would definitely need to have hardware spec ready.


So, like sensors, the lidars, the computing units, you would definitely need to upgrade it first before you can deliver this or achieve a certain functionality. So, we do believe that in the upcoming years, especially in China, I think all the car makers. Basically, they participate in this kind of arm race.


They would definitely keep upgrading the spec of the cars. So, the component size I think will benefit first. But in the mid- to long-term, of course, I think, the NAS can benefit from like a recurring revenue source. Probably they can monetize a service fee, license fee, or even like robotaxi operators that can be the mid- to long-term winners.


But in the next 12 to 18 months, we still believe that the hardware component side will see more meaningful value content upgrade opportunities.


**Laura Wang:** And let's bring that economics discussion to the humanoid space.


Where do you think the most profit will be preserved and kept within the humanoid industry?


**Sheng Zhong:** Yeah. Actually, I think what Tim mentioned for EV had a lot of learnings for humanoid, for robotics as well. So, in humanoid space, I think, it's similar. We also need a supply chain.


The upstream component, they will benefit first.


Because this downstream is very fragmented and diversified. But upstream they have a more consolidated suppliers, and they are benefiting from the scale first.


And then moving forward, the robot will be applied to the real economy. And, in the industry, it's already talking about the token, fees for robot as a possibility, and that maybe we can translate that to a service as well.


So, when the robot applies to the real scenario, the application service is also a profit pool for the industry. And in the end, we think the robot company that own the ecosystem from the robot development and also the application services will enjoy a very good profitability level.


**Laura Wang:** Thank you all for a great discussion.


**Robin Xing:** Thank you.


**Tim Hsiao:** Thank you.


**Laura Wang:** For those at home, if you enjoy Thoughts on the Market, feel free to share with a friend or colleague today.

## Transcript


**Serena Tang:** Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Serena Tang, Morgan Stanley's Global Cross-Asset Strategist.


**Seth Carpenter:** And I'm Seth Carpenter, Morgan Stanley's Global Chief Economist and Head of Macro Research.


**Serena Tang:** Today and tomorrow, a two-part conversation on Morgan Stanley's year ahead outlook.


Today, we'll focus on the global economy after a year of energy shocks and renewed inflation pressure. Tomorrow, we'll be back with our views on investing across asset classes.


It's Monday, November 16th at 10:00 AM in New York.


So Seth, let's start with the big picture.


It's been a challenging year to map the global economy with the war in Iran, shifting trade policies, and more recently, US midterms, adding uncertainty even as AI investment supports growth. As you look ahead to 2027, what's a story that ties it all together, and where do you see the global economy heading?


**Seth Carpenter:** Sure. I mean, the interesting thing I think so far might be a bit of a surprise, to date, about how, dare I use the word that's been overused a little bit, how resilient global growth has been.


We've had a whole series of shocks. We've had the energy price shock. Last year, we had tariffs. We've seen now developed market central banks starting to raise rates, and yet overall growth is holding up. And so we've titled the outlook this time, Powered by AI, Tested by Oil, because there really is this underlying momentum that's going on that is about this whole AI phenomenon.


In the United States, the build-out, the CapEx infrastructure spending is clearly strong, and it's one of the key drivers of US growth. But it's a global theme because Asia, where the world supply chain in many ways is located, is getting a lot of growth by exporting components for this build-out. Europe is actually getting into the game there a little bit as well, and Japan has been part of it.


So this AI phenomenon, that's global, and that's a big part of what's sustaining growth. But oil prices have gone up dramatically since the US invasion of Iran, and so we have to ask ourselves, what is going on with inflation? We've seen, headline inflation globally go up. We know that the spread of refined products over crude is higher than usual, so that risks more inflationary pressure coming through later.


And so we've seen central banks hiking in response. So the question becomes then, can this underlying momentum overcome the adverse shocks that we're seeing? I'd say our view is, yeah, probably. 2027 might see a little bit of a lull, a little bit of a slower pace initially, but that's not because we think we're actually going to have a real slowdown in the global economy.


It's just the growth rate this year is pretty strong. It's gonna be hard to top that regardless of what's going on.


To take that narrative and just to summarize it, to put it in numbers, to make it easier to digest, this year, global real GDP, we think, is tracking at about three and a half percent, so 3.5%. Next year, that little bit of a lull that I talked about would bring it down to something like 3.3% before rebounding in twenty twenty-eight to about 3.4%.


Now, that doesn't sound like a huge swing, and ultimately, we don't think it is. We are constructive about the growth rate of the global economy. But these little swings, especially when you think about it at a global level, can start to matter, and investors are gonna look at the data as they come in.


**Serena Tang:**


So you've given us the picture at the aggregate level. I actually want to dig a little bit more into the regional views. Where do you see faster growth? Where do you see slower growth? And what does inflation look like globally?


**Seth Carpenter:** Yeah, those are key, questions, and I think all of the conversations that I have with investors really touch on that. So I would say, first off, the US is clearly a key driver here, right?


So the AI CapEx build-out is absolutely taking place in the biggest part in the United States. And there we're looking for growth, call it two and a half to two and three quarters percent this year and about the same next year. So by US standards, that's really strong, growth numbers. Inflation, we think, is gonna stay high here as well.


We've seen the energy price shock feeding through. We know that the statistical agencies often have a little bit of what we call residual seasonality in the inflation data in the beginning of the year. And so we suspect that we're still gonna see a few more months of high inflation data. But if our forecast is right, and this is a critical if, if our forecast is right, Q1 will be the peak of inflation, and then we'll see it start to trend down in the United States because we do think growth remains solid.


But so far, we don't really see overheating going on in the labor market. Now, across the Atlantic in Europe, we're also pretty constructive. So a growth rate of around one and a quarter percent or so, of real GDP growth for Europe.


It's much less fast than what we're seeing in the United States, but nevertheless, it's holding up. That's being driven by a little bit of extra exports to the US, but fiscal policy clearly in Germany still supporting things, and the periphery is holding up in terms of overall demand.


Inflation there feels a lot like inflation in the United States. However, the economy is much more susceptible to, inflation energy price shocks. And so that's why the ECB started hiking before the Fed did.


We think there's probably another hike there. We also expect inflation there to drift down over time, but it's gonna take a while, and the divergence between the headline inflation numbers and the core inflation numbers might actually be a bit bigger in Europe than elsewhere.


Now, Asia. Asia's a really interesting story, and we're used to thinking of China as the other big economy in the world. And that's true, but their growth right now is on the tepid side by Chinese standards. We expect that to continue because they're still working through this debt deflation cycle.


And so four and a half percent or so, growth next year is about what we're looking for. We do think that deflation's going to ebb, but not anytime soon. That outcome is in contrast to the rest of Asia, especially take Korea, Taiwan, the real exporting houses for this whole AI CapEx build-out phenomenon.


Again, growth rates are gonna tell you a different story because the spending has been rising so rapidly now. We expect exports to stay very strong there. But in growth rate terms, it might actually come off, not because things are fundamentally weakening, but because you just can't keep that same pace of exporting going.


**Serena Tang:** So you touched on this earlier already, but as we know, inflation this year has driven a lot of debate around the Fed path.


So what are you expecting for 2027?


**Seth Carpenter:** Yeah, I mean, I think bring it back to the Fed and inflation, that really is the key story. On the growth side of things, things are holding up. We think the labor market is fine but not overheating, and so the whole story driving what the Fed's going to do comes down to inflation, like you said. So look, we expect, like the market does, another hike by the Fed in December.


We're looking for another hike in March. The market's gonna debate are they gonna slip another one in in January. But we don't think so. We think we've got two more hikes from here, December and March, and then that's it. What will it take for that forecast to come true? It's gonna mean that our inflation forecast also has to come true, which is to say firm inflation now, but no clear signs for an acceleration from here.


Because if things really pick up from here, then that January hike that the market's talking about might come true. It also means, though, that our forecast that Q1 is the peak of inflation in the United States and then it's a downward trend after that, that has to come true as well. Otherwise, it's entirely conceivable that the Fed would put in another hike after March, maybe in June, because they really want that assurance that inflation is coming down.


**Serena Tang:** And how you framed it just now, I think, is the important thing, right? What markets are pricing in versus our expectations. In which case, what is your most out-of-consensus view on the global economy in 2027?


**Seth Carpenter:** So I would say, you know, overall I don't know that we're wildly out of consensus anywhere. I would say we're probably above consensus in terms of our forecast for US growth. We are building in continued strong aggregate demand, but we're also penciling in an increase in the growth rate of productivity, partly because we do think, AI adoption is going on.


So that's one place where we're out of consensus. And then I guess I would come back to our discussion about inflation and what it means for central banks. The market is going to be debating a lot how much central banks are going to hike, how soon inflation's going to abate. Our view is, you know, Q1 is about the peak, and after that things come down, and so central banks won't have to hike more than that.


I would say if we're wrong, there are probably more paths to more rates from central banks and higher inflation than to lower. So I would say that's one place where I think our view maybe has a bit of tension with at least the way the market's trying to price things.


**Serena Tang:** Now, you've talked a lot about the base case. What are some of the alternate scenarios you see for the global economy?


**Seth Carpenter:** Yeah, I personally think it's critical to come into any round, forecasting round with a base case. But that only gets you so far. You really have to ask yourself, "How could we be wrong?" And so what we tried to do was to sketch out four alternate scenarios that have some of the key risks that we think are there in the economy and that we're talking to clients about in markets.


So in terms of a faster growth scenario, there really are two key, scenarios that we tried to analyze. One demand, demand for CapEx, demand for consumer spending, especially in the United States, where demand overall is just stronger than we think, and that outcome leads to faster growth, but it also leads to much higher inflation.


And so in response to that, the Fed and other developed market central banks are gonna have to raise interest rates more and maybe to the same peaks that we saw in the last hiking cycle coming off of the COVID inflation. On the other hand, we're trying to figure out how is AI adoption happening?


How much can productivity pick up? And so we also thought about a faster growth scenario where it's mostly driven by faster aggregate supply, that is, the productivity picks up faster. And the big difference there is that you're able to get faster growth without the same kind of inflationary pressures.


Now, central banks everywhere are going to see that, and the first thing they see is faster growth, Anytime you have faster growth from productivity, anytime the underlying potential growth rate of the economy is faster, it tends to mean that the neutral equilibrium interest rate is actually higher, and so you could get slightly higher interest rates than under the baseline, even though inflation is well-behaved.


Now, We, we are pretty constructive, and we do think there's probably more upside risk than downside risk, but we can't bury our heads in the sand. And so one version of the world is that the oil price shock that we've seen comes back, and we have oil prices going up a lot.


Central banks will see that, and they'll have to react to that. And the way that AI CapEx build-out is driving all of the growth right now, question that we get from clients a lot is: What would happen if that fell short of your expectations?


And I think that's worth thinking about too, because you have a combination of the direct spending, the direct effect of this build-out that's leading to more GDP, more growth, more exports from East Asia. But you also have an indirect effect, which is this whole phenomenon has driven up asset prices, which has given households more wealth, which has allowed strong spending to continue.


And so if those factors both went away, you would have a negative effect on the direct channel of spending and an additional drag on the economy from the indirect wealth channel. And for us, that means a slowdown. Probably not a recession. like I said, we're pretty constructive about what's going on with AI anyway, but one would have to at least consider what would happen if these spending plans fall short of our current forecast.


**Serena Tang:** And of course, all of those risk scenarios just means The range of outcome for risk assets is unusually wide.


**Seth Carpenter:** Yeah, I think that's right.


There is a huge amount of uncertainty here. We are in uncharted territory in so many ways. The AI phenomenon all by itself is just a brand-new situation for everybody in markets. But energy prices and everything that's going on in that space, there's still a lot of uncertainty.


We've had a series of these supply shocks and how that may or may not get embedded into inflation psychology in the way that price setters and price takers react to that inflation, that's uncertain as well. So I, I really think it is fair to say there's a very broad range of possible outcome here, and investors around the world are going to have to pay lots of attention.


**Serena Tang:** And of course, we're gonna be talking about that in our next podcast. Seth, thanks for taking the time to talk.


**Seth Carpenter:** Serena, it is always great to sit down with you and talk through these issues. I'm gonna turn the tables on you tomorrow and ask you about markets.


**Serena Tang:** Of course. And thanks to our listeners for joining. Please be sure to tune in to the second half of this conversation tomorrow to hear how we're thinking about investment strategy in the year ahead.

## Transcript


**Tom Wigg:** Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Tom Wigg from Morgan Stanley's TMT Specialty Sales. I'm joined by Joe Moore, U.S. Semiconductors Analyst, and Stephen Byrd, Global Head of Thematic Research.


Today, the disconnect between the AI power gigawatt shortfall, especially post-midterms, and a bullish outlook on AI semiconductors.


It's Friday, November 13th at 10am in New York.


Morgan Stanley already estimated a 30 gigawatt shortfall between now and 2028, and you revised that higher after the midterm. So maybe talk about our estimates, where they've gone now? And how you're thinking about this whole question around, you know, really Texas is kind of the ground zero for this conversation.


But it kinda happened in Ohio and other places as well…


**Stephen Byrd:** Absolutely. Yeah. I mean, obviously the election caused a lot of investors to focus on the political challenges, but this is not new per se. So, we've been talking about people, power, and politics being real bottlenecks on the ability to build out data centers in the United States.


Now, that creates a lot of incentive elsewhere around the world to build. But in the U.S., we have a lot of challenges in terms of the build-out. The election really underscored the importance of addressing data center concerns. A bunch of voters expressed concerns with data center development.


And to be fair, I think that's warranted in some cases because some of these data centers really are developed in ways that may not work for local communities. So, I understand the concern. Mathematically, what we essentially are looking at is that bottleneck getting larger in 2028 because of a couple of gubernatorial outcomes, Texas and Ohio being specific, where we think it's a delay.


It's not a cancellation. We actually think there's a path to getting these data centers built. It's just going to take a little bit longer because of the processes that those new governors are going to want data center developers to go through. So, we go from kind of 30 gigawatts up into the mid-30s in terms of the shortage.


But then in 2029, the deployment is much, much bigger. So, it is a relief valve, and in some ways – something Joe and I talk a lot about – helpful in some ways because this elongates that growth cycle as well.


**Tom Wigg:** What are the offsets that we can get? You know, \[be\]cause some clients will talk about, you know, Louisiana now became the new Texas that everyone…


**Stephen Byrd:** Yes.


**Tom Wigg:** … is excited about, you know; still a red state. Some clients are talking about Asia, particularly Malaysia as a region where labor's cheaper, there's no permitting. You know, maybe we can get a lot more gigawatts online.


**Stephen Byrd:** Mm-hmm. Yeah.


**Tom Wigg:** Google recently signed a deal there. Behind the meter, still an option. Grid optimization, probably not something I understand. But I know you've been a power exec, so maybe you do.


**Stephen Byrd:** Sure, sure.


**Tom Wigg:** Do you think we can kinda cobble together enough power in other ways where maybe your shortfall is too conservative?


**Stephen Byrd:** Yeah, I think there's a path where the shortfall is less than what we laid out, so let's go through all the options. But where there's a will and lots and lots of money and lots of innovation, there's often a solution.


So, let's go through the categories. So, off grid we like a lot, and we put in a forecast of what we think can be done in the United States. The challenge is time – in the sense that engineering those solutions, getting the labor, getting the permits, all of that takes time.


And an example, my home state of Virginia essentially outlawed on-site gas generation, in sort of anticipation that folks would go down this off-grid path. And they don't want to see those kinds of emissions.


So, we are running into challenges. When we tally that up, it's not as much power as I think many bulls would like. Just – it's not a question of demand, it's a question of all those challenges that I just mentioned. But there could be bigger solutions over time.


We have really good teams around the world that assess incremental demand and deployment. Just as you mentioned, Tom, Malaysia is one of those opportunities, though I would point to India, Thailand, a little bit in Japan, China.


On the other hand, we have issues in other parts of the world. So, Norway now has a moratorium on data centers. We're running into some problems in Australia. We're running into some problems in the United Kingdom, where a big, proposed UK project was terminated because the utility couldn't provide grid access fast enough.


So, it's a lot of puts and takes. When we add all this up, as of now, it's not enough to address the U.S. shortfall. But I would expect over time just more and more emphasis on getting solutions.


Now, one thing I do want to say where I'm not bullish is grid optimization. So, it's a cool idea. But let me just briefly explain why I think there's more hype than reality to this.


The idea is that the U.S. grid is actually only utilized on average, like, 50 percent of the time. Something like that, so there's clearly slack. The problem is that's not how a utility executive would look at the situation. Utilities manage the grid for the worst possible day or the worst possible situation. That would be a six-day winter storm, for example.
